The other trigger, threat, memory, and strategy items all center on generalized danger/hypervigilance and perpetrator-related reminders, not exposure/undress themes. Without any corroborating memory or appraisal content about forced stripping, searches, or sexualized humiliation, this item looks clinically mismatched.

vignette:
The event that fractured Mara’s world happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late October, during a routine call she had run a hundred times before. She was thirty-one, a paramedic with nine years on the job, and she had been dispatched to a domestic disturbance where a man had reportedly threatened his neighbor with a knife. When she arrived, the scene was already volatile—two officers had the man pinned against a chain-link fence, and he was screaming, thrashing, spitting. Mara’s job was to stand back, wait for the all-clear, then assess the neighbor for minor injuries. But the man broke free. He lunged past the officers, straight at her, and before she could raise her hands, he slammed into her chest, grabbed her by the collar of her uniform, and held a blade to her throat. She remembers the cold metal pressing into the soft skin under her jaw, the smell of sweat and cheap beer, the officer’s voice shouting “Drop it! Drop it!” and then the gunshot—a single, deafening crack that came from behind her. The man went limp. His blood sprayed across her face and neck. She stood there, frozen, the knife still in his dead hand, and she could not make sense of what had just happened. For weeks afterward, she could not tell the story. When her supervisor asked her to write an incident report, she sat at the keyboard for an hour, typing and deleting the same three sentences, unable to hold the sequence in her mind. The memories came in fragments—the cold metal, the shouting, the blood—but they arrived in the wrong order, or all at once, and when she tried to explain, her throat would close and she would lose the thread entirely. It still happens now, eight months later. She will be sitting in her living room, watching television, and suddenly she is back there, pinned against the fence, the blade against her throat, the gunshot ringing in her ears, and she has to physically shake her head to remind herself that it is over. The memory feels like it is happening right now, not like something that is finished.

Mara has not returned to work. She took medical leave after the first week, and then extended it, and then her divorce was finalized—a separation that had been coming for years but that the trauma seemed to accelerate, as if her husband could not tolerate the version of her that came home afterward. She lives alone now in a small apartment on the second floor, and she has arranged the furniture so that she can see the door from every seat. She always chooses where to sit based on how safe she feels—back to the wall, clear sightlines, an exit within reach. She scans constantly: the parking lot when she walks to her car, the hallway when she checks her mail, the grocery store aisles when she needs milk. It is exhausting, but she cannot stop. What frightens her most is being touched unexpectedly. A friend’s hand on her shoulder in a coffee shop sends her heart racing; a stranger brushing past her in a checkout line makes her flinch and gasp. She has come to believe that her body is no longer her own, that anyone could reach out and harm her at any moment, and so she keeps people at a distance. She avoids authority figures entirely—police cruisers make her pull over and wait until they pass, uniformed security guards in buildings make her turn around and leave. She has not been able to visit her own station, because the sight of her paramedic jacket hanging on the hook makes her stomach turn.

She has also learned to suppress her anger. She never allows herself to feel it, let alone express it, because she is certain that if she starts, she will not be able to stop, and she will become dangerous like the man who attacked her. When she feels the heat rising in her chest, she forces herself to breathe slowly, to smile, to say nothing. The nausea comes often now—a roiling in her stomach that she cannot tie to anything specific, just a constant low-grade queasiness that spikes whenever she feels stressed. She has stopped going out with friends. She has stopped returning calls. Her days are quiet and predictable, built around avoiding anything that might remind her of the person who harmed her, or the people in uniform who were supposed to protect her but instead shot a man two feet from her face. She came to therapy because her sister called her one night and found her sobbing on the floor, unable to explain why. What Mara hopes for, more than anything, is to stop feeling like the memory is still happening. What she is most afraid of is that she will never be able to leave that Tuesday afternoon behind.
